A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mergeability prediction framework and benchmark. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V4 reports original experiments on 190 model pairs, including LOTO prediction results, predictor and metric ablations, and gradient-regularized fine-tuning results.

after.justification: V6 reports original prediction and merging experiments across two ViT backbones, plus objective comparisons, metric ablations, and ten-seed optimization results.

M1.justification: The default predictor changes from dense, sum-to-one-constrained fitting to unconstrained Pearson-plus-L1 optimization with lambda=1. This sparse procedure already existed in v4 Appendix A.6, so it is not a newly introduced algorithm. An apparent gradient-feature substitution remains unresolved because v6 Appendix A.13.1 conflicts with A.3.5 and Table 8.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 20 image-classification datasets and pairwise merging task, as confirmed by v4 Appendix A.9 and v6 Appendix A.15. Adding ViT-B/32 expands model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated merger set changes from Task Arithmetic, Weight Averaging, TSV, and Isotropic to Task Arithmetic, Weight Averaging, TSV, TIES, and DARE, including in the fine-tuning experiment. V6 also adds an MSE-trained linear comparator in Appendix A.5. The MLP comparator already existed in v4.

E3.justification: V6 extends evaluation from ViT-B/16 to both ViT-B/16 and ViT-B/32 and adds an MSE optimization comparison. Primary prediction and category-ablation settings switch to L1 fitting. The fine-tuning regularization study changes from testing lambda values 0.001, 0.1, and 1 to reporting only 1. The 190-pair, 20-fold LOTO design and calibration sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V6 adds an objective-function ablation, optimization-initialization robustness tests, and gradient-contribution analyses explaining the TIES regularization exception. Existing L1, MLP, and metric-category analyses are revised or extended. V4's regularization-strength sweep and explicit top-10 metric-overlap matrix are removed.

E5.justification: V6 newly reports ten random initializations of L1 coefficient fitting, with across-seed means, standard deviations, ranges, and feature-selection stability in Tables 14–15. Fold-level uncertainty remains in Table 19 despite its omission from main Table 2. Conversely, the per-method MLP standard deviations in v4 Table 6 are no longer tabulated in v6 Table 13.

E6.justification: Primary prediction, coefficient, and ablation results are revised, with additional backbone, comparator, objective, and seed results. Under the respective analysis settings, average subspace/gradient ablation effects change from -0.123/-0.064 in v4 Table 14 to -0.045/-0.149 for ViT-B/16 in v6 Table 4. These are not same-setting performance gains. At lambda=1, reported Weight Averaging normalized accuracy changes from 96.47% to 96.25%; newly evaluated TIES decreases by 0.11 percentage points.

T1.justification: V6 removes the explicit sum-to-one constraint and associated coefficient-identifiability argument from Section 4. Its stable-metric criterion extends sign consistency from four mergers to ten merger/backbone combinations. The detailed metric formulas and gradient-penalty equation are retained, and the L1 formulation already appeared in v4 Appendix A.6.

C1.justification: The central claim that mergeability depends on partners and merging methods is retained. V6 qualifies fingerprint distinctiveness through shared method clusters, emphasizes gradients over the earlier joint subspace-and-gradient foundation, and extends its empirical generality claims to two backbones. These refine the existing contribution rather than replace its main thesis.

C2.justification: The interpretation shifts from primarily geometric subspace compatibility toward functional gradient compatibility. V6 adds architecture-dependent activation interpretations, cost-based metric recommendations, and a method-specific explanation of TIES's negative regularization result. Limitations more explicitly address data-free application and non-vision domains, but v4's warning that single-task degradation was not evaluated disappears.

D1.justification: V6 adds explicit TIES trimming, sign-resolution, and scaling settings; DARE dropping, rescaling, and fixed-seed information; and a computational-requirements discussion. It also newly documents validation-based early stopping for the MLP. Most existing calibration, optimizer, and fine-tuning hyperparameter tables are retained.

R1.justification: V6 adds the Yu et al. DARE reference and discussion of that method. Its positioning against intrinsic mergeability and black-box prediction remains largely unchanged. TIES was already cited; consolidating duplicate Wang references and updating publication metadata do not constitute additional research-positioning changes.

P1.justification: V6 substantially rewrites the results, stable-metric discussion, ablations, conclusion, and limitations around the sparse predictor. It reorganizes the appendices, expands explanatory passages, and places the conclusion before limitations. Much of the introduction, related work, and metric-definition prose remains shared.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to distinguish precomputed inputs, ground truth, and predictions. The earlier category-importance bar chart disappears; coefficient and selection heatmaps are reorganized into backbone-specific panels. The category-ablation table is also presented in the main text, and new cost, objective, seed-stability, and gradient-contribution tables substantially expand the displays.

improvement.justification: V6 strengthens validation through a second backbone, ten-seed stability tests, and an objective comparison. However, it introduces inconsistencies affecting its central interpretable signals: Appendix A.13.1 and the heatmaps replace encoder-gradient dot product with input-gradient magnitude ratio, while A.3.5 and Table 8 retain the earlier feature list. Tables 8 and 17 also disagree on leading metrics without identifying different settings. These reproducibility and interpretation problems, alongside reduced regularization-sensitivity and MLP-uncertainty reporting, prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
